=== Early life ===
Fisk was born in [[Washington, DC]], United States, on February 7, 1925, to Brenton Kern Fisk, a lawyer, and Amelia Worthington Fisk, a social worker and [[Women's suffrage|suffragette]].<ref name="Schuneman-1984" /> In the early 1930s, the Fisk family moved to the city of [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]].<ref name="The New York Times-1984">{{Cite news |date=January 10, 1984 |title=Memorial Service at Harvard set for Charles Brenton Fisk |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/01/10/arts/memorial-service-at-harvard-set-for-charles-brenton-fisk.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221224115404/https://www.nytimes.com/1984/01/10/arts/memorial-service-at-harvard-set-for-charles-brenton-fisk.html |archive-date=December 24, 2022 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> As a soprano, he joined the choir of the [[Christ Church (Cambridge, Massachusetts)|Christ Church]] of the [[Cambridge Common]], at which [[E. Power Biggs]] was the choirmaster<ref name="ahf.nuclearmuseum.org">{{cite web |title=Charles B. Fisk |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/charles-b-fisk/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221224121002/https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/charles-b-fisk/ |archive-date=December 24, 2022 |access-date=December 24, 2022 |website=[[National Museum of Nuclear Science & History]] |publisher=}}</ref> and organist.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Bishop |first=John |date=May 4, 2018 |title=In the Wind. ... |url=https://www.thediapason.com/content/wind-66 |access-date=November 24, 2024 |website=[[The Diapason]] |language=en}}</ref> At this point in life, Fisk reflected that his interest in organs had not matured yet, describing organs as simple "moaning in the background".<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Yocum |first=Keith R. |date=December 1979 |title=Charles Fisk, Organ Builder |journal=[[Country Journal]] |volume=6 |issue=12}}</ref>{{Rp|page=87}} In addition to singing, he played trumpets and organs.<ref name="ahf.nuclearmuseum.org" />

On Fisk's 13th birthday, he was gifted a reed organ, on which he made minor repairs.<ref name="preview">{{Cite thesis |last=Coffey |first=Mark Daryl |title=Charles Fisk: Organ Builder |date=May 1984 |access-date=March 1, 2023 |degree=Doctor |publisher=[[University of Rochester]], [[Eastman School of Music]] |url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/32fc412988eb674ab128af316518ea6d/ |url-access=limited |language=en |format=PDF |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230307175136/https://www.proquest.com/openview/32fc412988eb674ab128af316518ea6d/ |archive-date=March 7, 2023 |url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|page=2}} According to one of Fisk's friends, Fisk fiddled with electromechanical devices and built his own [[Amplifier|amplifiers]] when he was 14 years old.<ref name="ahf.nuclearmuseum.org" /> After playing his sister's Bach recordings on his amplifiers, he started to develop a fondness for the sound of organs. He was well-versed in creating [[tube amplifiers]], and acquaintances of Fisk's parents often asked for him to make one for them.<ref name=":7" />{{Rp|page=88}}

Fisk studied at [[The Cambridge School of Weston]] from 1938, and graduated in 1942.<ref name="The Boston Globe-1984" /><ref name="preview" />{{Rp|page=1}} In 1943, at age 17, he secured a job in the [[University of Chicago]]'s [[Metallurgical Laboratory]] with the help of his physicist uncle, [[Joyce C. Stearns|Joyce Stearns]], who also worked there.<ref name="ahf.nuclearmuseum.org" /><ref name="hell" /> Stearns had suggested to Fisk's parents that Fisk work with him to avoid being [[The draft|conscripted]] into the battlefields of [[World War II]].<ref name="preview" />{{Rp|page=2}}<ref name="hell" />

'''মো. তাহমিদুল ইসলাম''' (পরিচিতি নম্বর: ১৮৫৫৮), যিনি মাঠ প্রশাসনে '''ডা. মো. তাহমিদুল ইসলাম তমাল''' নামেও পরিচিত, হলেন একজন বাংলাদেশী সরকারি কর্মকর্তা এবং বাংলাদেশ সিভিল সার্ভিস (প্রশাসন) ক্যাডারের একজন সিনিয়র সহকারী সচিব। তিনি ৩৭তম বিসিএস পরীক্ষায় প্রশাসন ক্যাডারে দেশব্যাপী মেধা তালিকায় তৃতীয় (৩য়) স্থান অর্জন করেন।<ref name="mopa_gazette"/> তিনি শরীয়তপুর জেলার জাজিরা উপজেলার উপজেলা নির্বাহী অফিসার (ইউএনও) এবং কুড়িগ্রামের ভূরুঙ্গামারী উপজেলার সহকারী কমিশনার (ভূমি) হিসেবে দায়িত্ব পালন করেছেন।<ref name="bhurungamari"/><ref name="zajira"/>

== প্রারম্ভিক জীবন ও শিক্ষা ==
মো. তাহমিদুল ইসলাম বাংলাদেশের চাঁপাইনবাবগঞ্জ জেলায় জন্মগ্রহণ করেন।<ref name="rajshahi_div"/> তিনি মাধ্যমিক ও উচ্চ মাধ্যমিক সম্পন্ন করার পর রাজশাহী মেডিকেল কলেজে ভর্তি হন। তিনি কলেজের ৫০তম ব্যাচের শিক্ষার্থী হিসেবে ২০০৮-০৯ সেশনে চিকিৎসা শাস্ত্রে এমবিবিএস (MBBS) ডিগ্রি অর্জন করেন।<ref name="linkedin"/> 

== কর্মজীবন ==
=== চিকিৎসা পেশা ও বিসিএস স্বাস্থ্য ===
তাহমিদুল ইসলাম প্রথমে ৩৫তম বিসিএস (স্বাস্থ্য) পরীক্ষার মাধ্যমে সরকারি চাকরিতে সহকারী সার্জন হিসেবে কর্মজীবন শুরু করেন। চিকিৎসা পেশায় যুক্ত থাকাকালীন তিনি চিকিৎসকদের অধিকার ও জনসচেতনতামূলক প্ল্যাটফর্ম "প্ল্যাটফর্ম ফর মেডিকেল অ্যান্ড ডেন্টাল সোসাইটি" এবং চিকিৎসা বিষয়ক অনলাইন ম্যাগাজিন ''মেডিভয়েস''-এ কন্ট্রিবিউটর হিসেবে যুক্ত ছিলেন।<ref name="linkedin"/>

=== বিসিএস প্রশাসন ক্যাডার ===
পরবর্তীতে তিনি প্রশাসনিক সেবার মাধ্যমে বৃহত্তর পরিসরে কাজ করার লক্ষ্যে ৩৭তম বিসিএস পরীক্ষায় অংশ নেন। এই পরীক্ষায় তিনি বিসিএস (প্রশাসন) ক্যাডারে মেধা তালিকায় ৩য় স্থান অর্জন করেন এবং প্রশাসন ক্যাডারে যোগদান করেন।<ref name="mopa_gazette"/> 

মাঠ প্রশাসনে তাঁর পদায়নের উল্লেখযোগ্য বিবরণসমূহ নিম্নরূপ:
* '''সহকারী কমিশনার ও নির্বাহী ম্যাজিস্ট্রেট:''' প্রশাসন ক্যাডারে যোগদানের পর তাঁর প্রথম পদায়ন হয় খুলনা জেলা প্রশাসকের কার্যালয়ে।<ref name="khulna_div"/> পরবর্তীতে ২০২১ সালের আগস্টে এক আদেশে তাকে রাজশাহী বিভাগের নওগাঁ জেলা প্রশাসকের কার্যালয়ে বদলি করা হয়।<ref name="rajshahi_div"/> 
* '''সহকারী কমিশনার (ভূমি):''' ২০২৩ সালে তিনি কুড়িগ্রাম জেলার ভূরুঙ্গামারী উপজেলার সহকারী কমিশনার (ভূমি) বা এসিল্যান্ড হিসেবে দায়িত্ব নেন।<ref name="bhurungamari"/> সেখানে দায়িত্ব পালনকালে তিনি "স্মার্ট ভূমি সেবা সপ্তাহ" বাস্তবায়ন এবং স্থানীয় একটি চলাচলের রাস্তা সংক্রান্ত জটিল সামাজিক সমস্যা নিরসনে ভূমিকা রেখে প্রশংসিত হন।

The following is a list of people, songs, words, characters, and other media that have broken negative patterns. Sometimes there is no rule or theorem preventing a certain desired result, but seemingly by pure [[coincidence]], the desired result fails to occur over a seemingly long sequence of items. However, by the [[law of truly large numbers]], any result with a constant, non-infinitesimal probability is virtually guaranteed to happen in a sufficiently large sample or sufficiently long sequence. Sometimes, the first counterexample seems to be what we'd expect from a first counterexample: it satisfies the desired outcome but stops there. In other cases, the counterexample is practically perfect, as it, whether real or perceived, simultaneously breaks multiple curses or negative patterns that failed to be broken by any earlier items. The counterexample can, in a way, be said to be "above the rules," as the word "rule" here refers not necessarily to a deliberate rule or theorem but can also refer to a coincidental pattern. A "negative rule" refers to an undesirable or unfair pattern that coincidentally holds true for most or all items within a group to which the item belongs. 

Sometimes, for a list of criteria, we aim to find songs, words, celebrities, movies, etc., that satisfy one or more of the criteria on our list. For example, one may search for a musician who was "born in _______ (insert a year here)" and "plays the drums." Pokémon fans may try to find Pokémon that have a certain combination of traits, especially for the purposes of competitive battling or building a strong, viable in-game team for defeating the Elite Four. There is a Pokémon that satisfies the following: 1) It has a base "Defense" stat of 70, 2) It can have the ability "Shield Dust," 3) It was introduced in Ruby/Sapphire. If you guessed Dustox, you would be right, as it satisfies all three of these. 

Intuitively, the longer the list of criteria, or the harder each individual criterion is, the harder it is to find a perfect match satisfying all of them. The section below, titled "Examples," is not about ordinary counterexamples, where one particular unfair pattern was broken; this is about counterexamples that seem to be "above the rules" and seem to defy every negative rule or pattern that has existed, possibly coincidentally, for so long. Since the rule or pattern is unfair, it is a delightful miracle that the patterns have finally been broken, as justice has been served, at last. A notable example of a negative pattern or a negative absence was the fact that, prior to Generation 5, with the release of Pokémon Black and White in 2010 (Japan) or 2011 (rest of the world), Corsola was the only fully evolved Pokémon whose English name started with "CO," as in "coffee" or "cord." On the other hand, there were three fully evolved "CL" Pokémon, namely Clefable, Cloyster, and Claydol. This is a lexical imbalance, as there are far more "CO" words than "CL" words in the English language. You can easily verify this for yourself; go ahead, open a paper dictionary. In the Children's Dictionary that I got as a present for my eleventh birthday, in fifth grade, there were eight pages of "CL" words and thirty pages of "CO" words. That's roughly a 4:1 ratio! Generation 5 fixed this injustice, as it introduced not one, not two, but '''three''' Pokémon with "CO" names: Conkeldurr, Cofagrigus, and Cobalion. Although Corsola was a very weak Pokémon to have on your team, the three that were added in Generation 5 are all quite good. Generation 8 then gave us three more: Corviknight, Coalossal, and Copperajah, the first of which is both a competitive staple and a fan favorite. As I will discuss in the next section, Corviknight simultaneously broke several curses involving "CO" Pokémon. 

==Examples==
* '''Example 1: The "CO" Pokémon names.''' All right, I am going to continue my discussion of that example above by making it Example 1 in this section. Corsola had poor stats and was widely considered to be a terrible Pokémon to have on a team. In the first four generations, if you wanted to use a fully evolved "CO" Pokémon on your team, you were out of luck. Generation 5, which started in September 2010 (in Japan) and March 2011 (in North America), fixed this injustice by introducing three fully evolved "CO" Pokémon, like I mentioned before. And three really good ones at that. Cobalion is my favorite of these three, as it has a cool name, a cool design, and more. As a legendary Pokémon, it has amazing stats, with its base "Defense" and "Speed" stats both exceeding 100, being 129 and 108, respectively. It has a solid "Attack" of 90, which can be boosted with "Swords Dance," and then its "Sacred Sword" hits like a truck! Unfortunately, despite these traits, the community consensus is that Cobalion is not viable for competitive play. This is indicated by its low usage in OU, often being around 0.1% or 0.2%. It does get significant usage in "Monotype" formats, though. Generation 7 gave us Comfey, and then Generation 8 introduced Corviknight, Coalossal, and Copperajah. And of this trio, Corviknight is the one that breaks all negative rules and curses that previously existed for "CO" Pokémon.
** Corviknight is the first "CO" Pokémon to receive nearly universal praise by Pokémon fans. Cobalion has a rating of 42% on Tiermaker, but Corviknight has a rating of 77%.
** Corviknight, unlike Cobalion, sees very high usage in OU; for Generation 8 OU, it very consistently makes the top 20 in usage. In October 2021, it was #3 with a weighted usage of 21.52306%, behind only Dragapult and Landorus-Therian. It is worth noting, however, that Cofagrigus and Conkeldurr received ''somewhat'' high usage in Generations 5 and 6, at least sometimes. 
* '''Example 2: The "CA" Pokémon names.''' Calyrex, in its Shadow Rider form, breaks many former patterns about "CA" Pokémon. Believe it or not, prior to Generation 3, with the March 2003 release of Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire, the only "CA" Pokémon was Caterpie, and there were no fully evolved "CA" Pokémon. Caterpie, a Bug-type Pokémon you can find in the early game, evolves into Metapod, and then into Butterfree. Generation 3 fixed this lexical imbalance, introducing 135 new Pokémon. Three of those 135 Pokémon were Camerupt, Cacturne, and Castform. Wait, is it a coincidence that these all have 8 letters each? I think not! None of these Pokémon had a base "Speed" above 70; Camerupt and Cacturne had only 40 and 55, respectively. Generation 4 gave us Carnivine, which had a base "Speed" of 46. These Pokémon were not widely used in competitive play; last month, Camerupt, the highest of these, was #50 in Generation 3 OU, with only 0.76611% usage. In July 2015, back when "Sand Veil" was allowed, Cacturne saw only 0.44673% usage in Generation 4 OU. Generation 5 introduced Carracosta, and Generation 6 introduced Carbink. Now, there were six fully evolved "CA" Pokémon, none of which saw more than 0.5% usage. Going back to that same month, July 2015, the "highest" was Camerupt, at 0.16680%. In Generation 8, this streak was finally broken. On October 23, 2020, with the release of the Crown Tundra DLC for Pokémon Sword and Shield, Calyrex was introduced, and Calyrex-Shadow has a base "Speed" of 150 and a base "Special Attack" of 165. This makes Calyrex-Shadow the fifth fastest Pokémon in the game, tied with Electrode, Mega Aerodactyl, and Deoxys (Normal and Attack). In Generation 8 Ubers, it consistently made the top five in usage. In all twelve months of 2021, it was #3 with over 40% weighted usage, behind Yveltal and Necrozma-Dusk-Mane. It also made the top three in Generation 8 Anything Goes, with over 30% weighted usage in all twelve months of 2021. The same thing is true for 2022. In October 2022, it had 37.55022% usage. Statistically, the best combination of high stats is to have high "Attack" or "Special Attack" in combination with high "Speed." Calyrex-Shadow is absolutely no exception. Having high attacking stats and high speed is often a recipe for brokenness. This makes sense if you think about it: strong attacking stats allow the Pokémon to OHKO more opponents, and being extremely fast allows the Pokémon to do so before the opponent has a chance to move, since speed determines the turn order in battle. This is also why "Shell Smash" is such a powerful boosting move. His highest rated song was in the upper 70s, and none of the songs featuring him surpassed that record, either. Not Don Toliver. Not Wizkid. Not even "Where Are U Now" from 2015. I was very disappointed. But "Snooze" is above this rule. Even for the beloved, original version, Justin Bieber, while not present on the song, appears in the music video. 
** Back in July 2025, the "curse" of there being no Justin Bieber songs above 75% was still going. July 11, 2025, was a tough day for me. At 12:30 a.m., when I saw that he had released a new album and broken his hiatus, I eagerly checked the user score. When I saw that his new album, "Swag," got only 47%, I was very disappointed. I had waited three years for him to make his music comeback, and now that he finally did, he got yet '''another''' mediocre user score. The curse continued. Or so, I thought. There were still no counterexamples to the statement that "No song by Justin Bieber has a user score above 80%," but between his cameo in the "Snooze" video and the fact that the Justin Bieber remix got a passable, green rating, this was the song that was "closest" to being a counterexample. I worried I would have to wait another 2-3 years for his next album to '''hopefully''' see the curse broken, but luckily, it took only 2-3 months instead of 2-3 years, since "Speed Demon" has 84%. 
* '''Example 4: "Die With A Smile."''' Another song that broke multiple curses was "Die With A Smile" by Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars. There is generally a negative correlation between YouTube views and AOTY user scores, at least for videos above 500 million views. In 2023, two of the biggest songs on the radio were also two of the biggest songs on YouTube. Those were "Flowers" by Miley Cyrus and "Calm Down" by Rema and Selena Gomez. Both songs were rated in the 50s or 60s, indicating only a mixed reception, rather than a brilliantly warm reception as enjoyed by "Save Your Tears" and "Leave the Door Open" from 2021 or Taylor Swift's "Style" from 2015. "Baby Shark," the most viewed video, with over 16 billion views, has a rating of only 10%, based on 326 user ratings. Next is "Despacito," also rated below half. In fact, if you look at Wikipedia's list of the {{w|List of most-viewed YouTube videos|most watched YouTube videos}}, you can see "Shape of You," which also has a terribly low user score, "See You Again," also not a fan favorite, and several Cocomelon songs. You have to go down to '''number NINE''' before you reach the first well-received song on this list: "Uptown Funk." At 5.8 billion views, this video has barely one-third of the number of views "Baby Shark" has. "Die With A Smile," unlike most songs in recent years (2021 or later) that had surpassed a billion views, has a very high user score: 80.3% as of December 2025, based on 2,352 user ratings. The rating has been tanking slightly over time, having fallen 9 points per thousand since September 1, 2025, when it was at 81.2%. The universal level of acclaim for "Birds Of A Feather," a similar song about loving someone for the rest of one's life, as well as "Not Like Us," makes sense, as those songs have 824 million views and 470 million views, respectively, as of 12/17/2025, are still "within reason," despite being very high view counts, though nowhere near as high as "Die With A Smile," at 1.4 billion. Although Todd did not put the song on last year's "Best Hit Songs" list, he called it a "decent" song during the section for his number 9 pick, "II Most Wanted." However, knowing my luck, he might put it on the "worst hit songs" next week, as a dishonorable mention, as I do strongly associate this song with my imaginary friend, and every time I hear the song on the radio, I think of him. Still, the fact that this song gets an 81% makes it yet another counterexample to my original conjecture that a "connection to my imaginary friend" makes people dislike the song. Another 2024 song with this trait is Ariana Grande's "We Can't Be Friends," released on March 8, 2024, with well over 300 million views to date. I associate that song with my imaginary friend, and it has a rating of 82% based on 474 user ratings. And what's more, it reminds me of [https://www.innseason.com/riverwalk-resort River Walk Resort], a hotel and resort in Lincoln, New Hampshire, that I've visited three times and greatly enjoyed on all three visits. I love the backyard swimming pool and the hotel's design, both inside and outside, and in my head, this song is now the "theme song" for that resort.
* '''Example 5: "Bad Romance."''' As of May 21, 2026, "Baby Shark" is, by far, the most viewed YouTube video, with 16,943,408,827 views. No other YouTube video comes CLOSE to that. The next highest is "Despacito," at 9,022,649,778 views. "Baby Shark" has held this crown since November 2, 2020, so it has been 5 years, 6 months now. The "Historical most-viewed videos" section of the page [[List of most-viewed YouTube videos]] shows a table of the videos that formerly held the crown. Neither "Baby Shark" nor "Despacito" breaks 50% on ''Album of the Year.'' "Baby Shark" has a user score of 10%, while "Despacito" has 38%. A score of 10% is '''terrible''' by ''Album of the Year'' standards. Unfortunately, "See You Again," which held the crown for 25 days in the summer of 2017, has a middling rating, too. The same is true for "Baby," which is in the 40s. However, "Bad Romance," which held the crown for three months back in 2010 (April 14 through July 16), has an astonishingly high 92% rating, indicating "nearly universal acclaim." In May 2010, "Bad Romance" became the first video to reach 200 million views on YouTube. This song is privileged as it, unlike most of the other former holders of the title of most viewed video, has an extremely high user score. In terms of user score, it's a night-and-day difference between "Bad Romance" and "Baby Shark." "Bad Romance" is a highly renowned counterexample to the negative correlation between views and user satisfaction. As amazing and magical as it is that "Die With A Smile" has simultaneously high viewership and high acclaim, "Bad Romance" takes this a step further by being a former "most viewed video" while also enjoying a 90%+ user score. Much like "Die With A Smile," this is another song with very special, exclusive privileges and exemption from rules and unfavorable correlations that sadly apply to most songs. "Bad Romance" is a perfect song. Today, the same is also true, to a lesser degree, to "Gangnam Style," which currently has a score of 83%. I've been using AOTY for four years, and out of the hundreds of songs I've studied and collected in a Notepad file for my research, this is perhaps the "most improved" song on the site. It was only at 59% back in January 2022 when I first started using the site, and it has now risen more than 20 percentage points!
** "Bad Romance" was blessed in another way, too. [[Special:Diff/614995461]] is from June 30, 2014. See that diff to see what the most-viewed videos were at the end of June 2014. Back then, "Gangnam Style" was number one, at 2.02 billion views, without competition, with Justin Bieber's "Baby" being #2 with barely half of that, with 1.05 billion views. However, by that point, neither song was being played on any of my three go-to radio stations (103.3, 104.1, 107.9). The last time Mix 104.1 played "Gangnam Style," as far as I can tell, was around 4 or 5 in the afternoon on January 1, 2013, only six months after the song came out. And I didn't get to hear "Baby" on the radio at all. I was also not hearing "On The Floor." But "Bad Romance" was still being played on Mix 104.1 and other stations. For much of the second half of 2014 and the first half of 2015, I had the following conjecture: "If the music video has too many views, it's not allowed on these radio stations." I was relieved to hear "Love The Way You Lie" on August 3, 2014, two days before the fourth anniversary of the music video, at the time the #5 video on YouTube with over 700 million views. "Bad Romance" was #10 with 590 million at the end of June 2014. That's only 29% of the 2.02 billion vies that "Gangnam Style" had! So, clearly, "Bad Romance" was "fair game," and therefore, 590 million was not "too high." Hearing Eminem's song meant that 700 million wasn't off-limits, either. At the time, there were no counterexamples, but little did I know, there would be TONS of counterexamples just a year and a half later. Now, take a look at [[Special:Diff/697660542]] from 23:53 UTC, 31 December 2015. The first thing to note is that "Baby" is no longer #2. It's not even #3. Now, it's #4. "Blank Space" and "See You Again" were now at #2 and #3, respectively. And both of those songs remained strong on the radio. The same thing can be said about "Uptown Funk," which was #5, "Thinking Out Loud," which was #21, with 909 million views. Even down at number 21, "Thinking Out Loud" was no slouch when it came to views, exceeding the June 2014 "limit" of 700 million by nearly 30%, roughly 28%.
** "Bad Romance" is part of what I call the "2010 blessing." On April 14 of that year, "Bad Romance" surpassed the "Charlie bit me" video to become YouTube's most viewed video. At the time, "Bad Romance" had 178,400,000 views. That April date was exactly one month after March 14, 2010, the release date of Pokémon Heart Gold and Soul Silver, often abbreviated as "HGSS." While most of the newer Pokémon games have low user scores on Metacritic, HGSS have scores of 9/10; both games have 1,400+ ratings each, and they are tied at 9.1/10 for being the highest rated mainline Pokémon games. This is in sharp contrast to recent titles such as Pokémon Scarlet/Violet from 2022, with 3/10 and Sword/Shield from 2019, with 4.7/10. Today, many Pokémon fans on Reddit have given up on the franchise, with the opinion that the franchise peaked in 2010 with HGSS and will "never make another good game again." I, for one, strongly hope that 2027's Wind/Waves game will break the "curse" and get 8/10 or 9/10 again.
